::: {.callout-important}
## Why this shows up on TMUA

Paper 2 asks the **Prf4** type as multiple choice: *"the lines of a proof are given in the wrong order —
which ordering is correct?"* You never write the proof; you **judge the logical flow**. The skill is
finding the one line that must come first, the one that must come last, and then respecting the
**dependencies** in between.
:::

::::: {.formulasheet}

:::: {.fs-head}
<div class="fs-kicker">TMUA · Paper 2 · Mathematical Reasoning · Prf4</div>
<div class="fs-title">Scrambled Proofs — Key Concepts</div>
<div class="fs-sub">A jumbled list of statements has to be reassembled into a valid proof. Anchor the two ends — the opening line and the conclusion — then order the middle by "what does each line need before it can be said?"</div>

## Reassembling a proof

:::: {.fs-grid}

::: {.fs-card}
### Find the first line

The opening line **sets up**, it never concludes. Look for:

$$\textbf{"Let…"}\quad\textbf{"Suppose…"}\quad\textbf{"Assume…"}\quad\text{a definition / given}$$

[a proof by contradiction opens with **"Assume the statement is false"**]{.eg}
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### Find the last line

The final line is the **conclusion** — the thing you set out to prove, or the contradiction that settles
it.

$$\textbf{"…which is even."}\quad\textbf{"…a contradiction."}\quad\textbf{"…so } S \text{ is true."}$$

[anchor both ends first; the middle then almost orders itself]{.eg}
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### The dependency rule

Every line must be **justified by what comes before it**. A line that **uses** a quantity or a result
must come **after** that quantity is introduced or that result is established.

[you cannot write "so $a=2c$" before the line that says "$a$ is even"]{.eg}
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### Read the connecting words

The linking words fix the order:

**"Let / Suppose"** → opening. **"Since / Because"** → points **back**. **"Therefore / So / Hence"** →
follows from the lines **above**. **"But this contradicts…"** → near the end.
:::

::::

## The shape of each proof type

:::: {.fs-grid}

::: {.fs-card}
### Direct proof

**Assume/represent** the objects → **algebra/steps** → **state the conclusion**. The order is the order of
the algebra.
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### Proof by contradiction

**Assume the opposite** → derive consequences → **reach something impossible** → **conclude the statement
is true**. The "contradiction" line is always second-to-last.
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### Where it shows up (cross-exam)

Prf4 on Paper 2; the same "put the argument in order" skill is tested in **MAT/STEP** structured proofs
and in comprehension questions.
:::

::::

:::::

:::: {.fpnotes}

## True or false? — test yourself

Facts about how a proof is ordered. Memorise the verdict; **the *False* ones are the traps.**

| Statement | T / F ? |
|---|:--:|
| A line that uses a previously-derived result must come **after** that result. | |
| In a proof by contradiction, the opening line **assumes the statement is false**. | |
| The **last** line of a proof is its conclusion. | |
| "Therefore" signals a line that **follows from** the lines above it. | |
| "Suppose" or "Assume" usually signals an **opening** line. | |
| The **first** line of a proof states what you are trying to prove. | |
| In a direct proof of "if $P$ then $Q$", the first line assumes $Q$. | |
| The lines of a valid proof can be put in **any** order and stay valid. | |

## Proofs of the "true or false?" facts

Decide each verdict above first, then open the key.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Answers & proofs
- A line that uses a previously-derived result must come **after** it — **True**: a step is valid only once the things it uses have appeared.
- In a proof by contradiction, the opening line **assumes the statement is false** — **True**: that is the method.
- The **last** line of a proof is its conclusion — **True**.
- "Therefore" signals a line that **follows from** the lines above — **True**.
- "Suppose" / "Assume" usually signals an **opening** line — **True**.
- The **first** line states what you are trying to prove — **False**: the first line **sets up** (a Let/Suppose/given); the goal is where you **end**.
- In a direct proof of "if $P$ then $Q$", the first line assumes $Q$ — **False**: it assumes **$P$**.
- The lines of a valid proof can be put in **any** order and stay valid — **False**: order is everything — each step needs its inputs already present.
:::

## Notes

### The method: anchor the ends, then follow the dependencies

Never try to read a scrambled proof top-to-bottom. Do this instead:

::: {.keyline}
**1.** Find the **first** line — a "Let / Suppose / Assume" or the given. &nbsp; **2.** Find the **last**
line — the conclusion or the contradiction. &nbsp; **3.** Fill the middle so that **each line is justified
by the ones above it** (a line using "$a=2c$" comes after "$a$ is even").
:::

::: {.example}
[Example.]{.lbl} These four lines prove "the sum of two odd numbers is even", but they are jumbled. Put
them in the correct order.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(i)** So the sum is $2(a+b+1)$, which is even.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(ii)** Let the two odd numbers be $2a+1$ and $2b+1$.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(iii)** Their sum is $(2a+1)+(2b+1)=2a+2b+2$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution
Order: **(ii), (iii), (i).** &nbsp; (ii) is the opening "**Let…**"; (i) is the conclusion "…which is
**even**"; (iii) is the algebra that must sit between them, since (i)'s "$2(a+b+1)$" is only reached after
(iii)'s "$2a+2b+2$". $\;\blacksquare$
:::

::: {.workbox}

:::

### Contradiction proofs — the tell-tale ends

For a contradiction proof the ends are unmistakable: the **first** line is "**Assume … is false**" (or
"Suppose $\sqrt2=a/b$ in lowest terms"), and the **last two** lines are "**… a contradiction**" then "**so
the statement is true**". Order the middle by the chain of consequences.

::: {.example}
[Example.]{.lbl} These lines prove "$\sqrt2$ is irrational". Put them in order.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(i)** Then $4c^2=2b^2$, so $b^2=2c^2$ and $b$ is even.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(ii)** Suppose $\sqrt2=\dfrac ab$ in lowest terms.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(iii)** So $\sqrt2$ is irrational.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(iv)** Then $a^2=2b^2$, so $a$ is even; write $a=2c$.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(v)** But now $a$ and $b$ share the factor $2$ — a contradiction.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution
Order: **(ii), (iv), (i), (v), (iii).** &nbsp; Opening assumption (ii); then "$a$ even" (iv) must precede
(i) because (i) uses $a=2c$; (i) gives "$b$ even"; (v) is the contradiction (needs both $a,b$ even); (iii)
concludes. $\;\blacksquare$

*The dependency $\text{(iv)}\to\text{(i)}$ is the whole question: you cannot substitute $a=2c$ before you
have written it.*
:::

::: {.workbox}

:::
